flashcards.q: State the write-ahead logging rule in one sentence.
flashcards.a: The log record for a change must be durable before the corresponding data page is allowed to reach disk, and the commit log record must be durable before the client is told the transaction committed.

flashcards.q: Name ARIES's three recovery phases and what each does.
flashcards.a: Analysis: scan from last checkpoint, build Transaction Table + Dirty Page Table, find where redo must start. Redo: replay ALL changes forward (committed and uncommitted) - 'repeat history'. Undo: roll back uncommitted transactions in reverse order using Compensation Log Records.

flashcards.q: What is a pageLSN and how does it make redo idempotent?
flashcards.a: pageLSN is the LSN of the last log record reflected in a given page. Redo skips any log record whose LSN <= the page's current pageLSN, so already-applied changes are never reapplied - safe to rerun recovery from scratch.

flashcards.q: Why does redo replay changes from uncommitted transactions too?
flashcards.a: At analysis time you can't cheaply/correctly determine what's 'needed' without the state you're reconstructing. Redo is deliberately blind ('repeat history'); undo removes the effects of transactions that never committed afterward.

flashcards.q: What is a Compensation Log Record (CLR) and why does undo need it?
flashcards.a: A CLR logs each undo action itself, so a crash during recovery's undo phase doesn't lose track of progress. It makes undo replayable and idempotent, matching the guarantees of the forward log.

flashcards.q: What is a checkpoint's actual purpose?
flashcards.a: Solely to bound recovery time by giving analysis a recent starting point (the oldest recLSN of any dirty page as of the checkpoint) instead of scanning from the start of the log. Not for saving disk space.

flashcards.q: What is the most common real-world cause of WAL directory filling up disk?
flashcards.a: A disconnected or stuck replication slot (physical or logical) retaining WAL segments because its consumer isn't reading them, preventing log truncation.

flashcards.q: Name two real fsync 'lies' that cause silent data loss.
flashcards.a: A volatile disk write-back cache (no battery backing) can ack a write before it's physically durable. The 2018 Linux kernel fsync-error-handling bug cleared the dirty-page error flag after a failed fsync, letting a later fsync call falsely report success.

flashcards.q: Why do databases PANIC on fsync failure instead of retrying?
flashcards.a: Because of documented kernel behavior where a retried fsync after a failure can report false success, silently discarding data the app believed was durable. PANICing (crashing) is the defensive alternative to that risk.

flashcards.q: What is group commit and what does it optimize?
flashcards.a: Batching multiple transactions' WAL records into one fsync call instead of one fsync per commit, amortizing the fixed fsync latency across many transactions - often an order-of-magnitude throughput gain under concurrency.

flashcards.q: Postgres synchronous_commit on vs off - what's the tradeoff?
flashcards.a: on: fsync WAL before acking commit (full durability, higher latency). off: ack before fsync completes, risking loss of the last fraction-of-a-second of acked commits on an OS/machine crash, in exchange for throughput.

flashcards.q: InnoDB innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit values and their meaning?
flashcards.a: 1 = fsync every commit (full ACID durability). 2 = write to OS cache every commit, fsync ~once/sec (survives mysqld crash, not OS crash). 0 = write+fsync ~once/sec regardless of commits (fastest, can lose ~1s of transactions).

flashcards.q: What does Postgres full_page_writes protect against, and what's its cost?
flashcards.a: Torn pages - a crash mid-write leaving a page partly old/partly new bytes, which normal WAL replay can't repair. Cost: WAL volume spikes right after every checkpoint since the whole page is logged on its first post-checkpoint write.

flashcards.q: Why is kill -9 not a valid test of durability guarantees?
flashcards.a: It doesn't interrupt in-flight disk writes or lose OS page cache the way a real power loss does. A valid test pulls power or fault-injects mid-write and verifies exactly what was acknowledged survived.

flashcards.q: Why did WAL win over shadow paging as the dominant recovery architecture?
flashcards.a: Shadow paging gives crash safety via copy-on-write + atomic root swap but destroys physical locality over time and complicates fine-grained concurrent transactions. WAL keeps pages in place, preserving locality and allowing independent row/page-level locking or MVCC.
